did.unittitle: Lowell Thomas Papers: Graphic Materials

repository.corpname: Marist University Archives and Special Collections

did.abstract: The Lowell Thomas Papers encompasses a wide range of materials documenting the life, family, and professional career of Lowell Thomas. These materials include correspondence, administrative and financial documents, manuscripts, printed materials, photographic materials, motion picture films, audio recordings, and memorabilia.
did.langmaterial: The language of the materials is predominately English. Other languages include:Arabic,Chinese, French,German, Hebrew,Hindi, Italian,Spanish and Swedish.

scopecontent.head: Collection Overview
scopecontent.p: This series is includes glass plate negatives, lantern slides, photographic prints, film negatives, transparencies, photograph albums, postcards, stereographic cards, sketches and oversize graphic materials. These materials relate primarily to Lowell Thomas's professional projects, but the series also includes many images of Thomas's family, friends, and sporting activities. Of particular interest are the images created by Frank Roberson, the noted photographer with whom Thomas collaborated on his travelogues. This series is divided into three subseries arranged by form of material. Further subdivisions (sub subseries, etc.) are arranged by form of material or alphabetically by subject. A project to digitize these materials with the support from the National Historical Publications and Records Commission (NHPRC) was successfully completed on October 2012. And as a part of the project all the digitized 40,000 images are made available for the researchers through the online finding aids.

acqinfo.p: The Lowell Thomas Papers were donated to Marist University by the Thomas family in 2006.

bioghist.head: Historical Note
bioghist.p: Lowell Jackson Thomas was born in Woodington, Ohio on 6 April 1892 to two school teachers, Harry G. Thomas and Harriet Wagner Thomas. The family did not remain in Darke County, Ohio for very long because Lowell's father wanted to become a doctor. Harry G. Thomas's pursuit of a medical degree led the family to Kirkman, Iowa where five-year-old Lowell was enrolled in school for the first time. Harry's studies soon led him to the University of Nebraska. Upon graduation, Harry G. Thomas followed his brother's suggestion to begin his medical practice in the twin mining boom towns of Cripple Creek and Victor, Colorado. It was here in the rugged American West that Lowell spent the better part of his childhood and young adult years.

arrangement.head: Arrangement of the Collection
arrangement.p: These records are organized into three series: 1. Photographs, 2. Sketches, and 3. Oversize graphic materials. Series 1, has nine subseries. Subseries 1.1 has two subseries, 1.1.1 has 32 subseries, 1.1.1.13 has four subseries and 1.1.1.25 has two subseries; subseries 1.1.2 has twelve subseries, 1.1.2.1 has nine subseries. Subseries 1.2 has twelve subseries, 1.2.1 has seven subseries, 1.2.4 has 36 subseries, 1.2.4.3 has two subseries, 1.2.4.21 has three subseries, 1.2.4.23 has three subseries; 1.2.11 has two subseries, 1.2.12 has two subseries. Subseries 1.3 has six subseries. 1.3.1 has three subseries, 1.3.1.1 has eight subseries, 1.3.1.3 has two subseries; 1.3.3 has four subseries. Subseries 1.4 has three subseries, subseries 1.5 has two subseries, subseries 1.9 has five subseries, 1.9.1 has two subseries. Series 2 has two subseries. Series 3 has eleven subseries. Subseries 3.3 has four subseries, subseries 3.8 has two subseries.

note.p: The Marist University Archives and Special Collections staff wishes to express their deep appreciation to all of the parties that helped the Lowell Thomas Project come to fruition.

scopecontent.p: Series contains Lowell Thomas Indexed photographs, Alaska, images produced by August Heydey (colorist), images from commerical photographers and colorists, images of the German Revolution, Hammersley Hill (NY), Italy, Military, Mount Everest, Near East, First World Flight, and Miscellaneous Lantern Slides.

scopecontent.p: Series contains Arabia, Palestine, Egypt, Personal, Malaya, Burma, and India

South side of moat, sunset

Verso: Moat originally 25 ft. deep and 100 ft. wide. Was once covered with large pink lotus lilies. After annexation in 1885 the British military authorities destroyed the lotus to prevent malaria. They haven't succeeded yet. Some lotus left. They keep destroying plants over and over. Roots, or suckers, are imbedded in ground and only way to drive out the lotus is to dry moat absolutely. Malaria is not bad here today though. Burmese love the lotus roots as vegetable food. Slightly similar in taste to turnip. Moat and walls were built by town ministers under Mindon. Each man had his own portion. This done to produce spirit of rivalry. Mindon impressed people into the work.

Nan Oo Pagoda

Verso: To the east of the palace. Built by Mindon in 1857. There is always a pagoda to the east of every royal palace and facing the palace. On the north side there must also be a capinile or watch tower. Must be built simultaneously. All three must be finished at the same hour all at a given signal in the presence of the reigning king. Mr. H. C. Noyce says Col. Sladan's butler got drunk and went up in pagoda and kicked up a big row and he had to arrest him.
Burma
Royal Palace from the East

Verso: Royal palace from East, entrance to throne room. This palace was where audiences were held. Was built by Mindon. It was in this palace that Thebaw surrendered. Col. Sladan, who had been political resident in Mandalay, entered before troops. Mindon Min built a church and school for the church of Eng. for Dr. Marlas and sent the princes there including Thebaw. King and Queen Thebaw and Supyalat seldom ever left palace. Queen only went out 3 times. Afraid of assassins.
Burma
Royal Palace from the East with troops in the foreground

Verso: Eastern view of Royal Palace. Built of teals from the Shiveli forest in the Katha district where the finest teak comes from. Roofed with corrugated iron. British government has put in new foundations of concrete but lightning or earthquake might bring it down. Not a big earthquake here since 1839 which split the great Mingun Pagoda. It is one of the finest symmetrical buildings in Burma. Rises very gracefully from base. For carving the Queen's monastery built by Supyalat is finest example of carving altho not so symmetrical. In 1885 monastery was [?] of gold.
Burma
Royal Palace from the East, distant view

Verso: These cannon were presented by the French government to the Burmese government in days of King Pagan Min (the famous cock fighter whose capital was Amurapura.) He was defeated by his younger bro. Mindon who brought them to Mandalay. Mindon, after defeating his bro., treated him with great respect and enabled him to live royally to his death. Mindon was greatest of late Burman rulers. To please Queen Victoria he encouraged Christianity and built Christ Church. No war between Burma and Britain in his day. He sent an embassy to London to tell Queen Victoria he had done this meritorious act on her behalf. In return the Queen sent out a marble fount for Baptismal purposes which stands in the church today.
Burma
Three tombs, branches above

Burma
Three tombs, no branches above

Verso: Central tomb is where King Mindon was buried. Tomb on right is Queen Ain ByerMahyin, mother of Thebaw. (Owner of the White House) Tomb on left is where Queen Sinbyoo May Yin, (which means owner of a white elephant), mother of Supyalat. She was the intriguer and responsible for all the massacres in Oct. 1879, including 50 or 60 of the royal house. Supyalat sided with her mother but was only about 17 yrs. old although queen at the time. All of Thebaw's step bros. wanted to be king so it was done in defense of throne.
Burma
Thebaw Kyaung with wife of Ou Chit Pwe dancing, Lowell Thomas with pith helmet, umbrella and cane

Verso: King Thebaw's Kyaung- built by Mindon and where his son Thebaw rec'd his theological training. He was there until he was selected for the throne. It was done by lot but there was trickery on part of Supyalat's mother and she worked things so that he was the lucky man. He was not the eldest son and not even the son of the favorite queen. Thebaw was about 21 when he became king. Before then he was unknown. He was a handsome Burman, with round face, heavy mustache, and very heavy set. Not much intelligence doing. He let his mother in law and wife run things. Supyalat overrode king's ministers. There was talk among the ministers of Thebaw being too young and weak. Supyalat heard of this and put out all the ministers but one and he was the Prince minister who agreed to kneel before her golden foot. But he was the only high Burman official who tried to prevent the 3rd Burmese war. He had been to Eng. and knew Eng's power but others wouldn't listen. British gave him a pension until he died. Thebaw in monastery 2 or 3 years. British used it as a church of England for troops. Now going to ruin which is most unfortunate.

Note: This iron fence encloses the spot famous in history as "the Black Hole of Calcutta." The palace of an Indian prince stood here long years ago. In it was a room the exact size of this enclosure, in which the Rajah imprisoned nearly two hundred Europeans. When the door was opened the next morning most of them were dead from suffocation. That tragedy led to one of the ten decisive battles in the history of the world, the Battle of Plassey, where Clive overthrew the Moghul emperor

Mohammed Dali Khan (Afghan minister for foreign affairs) in full dress

Verso: Afghanistan - No.59; Vali Muhammad Khan, Afghan Minister for Foreign Affairs. Although the Amir has never been out of his country, this member of his cabinet has recently returned from a world tour. Among other countries he visited the United States hoping to be able to get the President to send a permanent diplomatic official to the Amir's capital. Although Afghanistan has long been a forbidden land the new ruler is so anxious that his country shall play a prominent part in world affairs that he is inviting foreign powers to send ministers. It is rumoured the Afghan minister for Foreign Affairs considered he was shabbily treated in Washington because he was not officially recognized, although finally did meet President Harding and Secretary of State Hughes, informally. But America has not decided to send a diplomatic officer to the Amir's court. Nevertheless the American Charge d'Affairs at the Court of the Shah of Persia was asked to find out all he could about Afghanistan and make a report. It was through him that Mr. Lowell Thomas was at last successful in his wish to penetrate into the land of the Afghans. - He is acting as King in the Amir's absence at present!

L.T. and the private river steamer he used on one of his recent expeditions in Southern Asia. Note: The Irrawady River is one of the mighty rivers of the earth. It is to the Asiatic country of Burma what the Mississippi River is to the central states of U.S.A. In fact it is even more, because it is the principal artery of travel. To a considerable extent the life of Burma flows up and down the mighty Irrawady. For more than a thousand miles, as you journey up the river from the Bay of Bengal, from Rangood to Mandalay, you are never out of sight of the Burmese Pagoda, a Buddhist place of worship. Lowell Thomas and his party used this special river steamer as their base on an expedition which took them far up the Irrawady, and on many side trips into the jungle.

On the remote and seldom visited southwestern coast of India, in the ancient seaport of Cochin, we found an extraordinary colony of Jews. Their patriarchs told us that their ancestors were exiled to this part by ancient Babylonian King Nebuchadnezzar. By these Jews are now divided into two groups, one called the white Jews and the other the black. Their customs are the same as the customs of the ancient Israelites of thousands of years ago. Lowell Thomas Travelogues

Afghanistan - No. 28; Between the cities of Jellalabad and Kabul the party stopped for one night at the mountain village Nimlah in one of the Amir's rest - houses. This was surrounded by a high wall and a beautiful park of cypress trees. The trees were said to have been planted by the Emperor Jahangir, one of the great Moghuls. In addition to the avenues of symmetrical trees, there are gardens and fountains similar to those around the Taj Mahal. The reception which Mr. Lowell Thomas and party received here reminded them that they had left behind lands where European customs are prevalent. A midnight dinner fit for an oriental monarch was prepared for them. Eight swarthy Central Asians, with baggy trousers, huge turbans and slippers with upturned toes, came in single file each bearing a silver slaver covered with Afghan viands seasoned with spice and garlic. The last course included slabs of watermelon, and grapes that California would be proud of. Then squads of soldiers camped in a circle around the beds of the Amir's guests which were spread on the lawn. The soldiers were there to see to it that no prowler came near with his knife

Afghanistan - No. 37., Through the heart of the Amir's capital runs the historic Kabul River. The main bazaar commences at this point. The bridge in the distance is covered over after the fashion of the Ponte Vecchio over the Arno at Florence. On both sides are the stalls of sandal sellers and of vendors of bright coloured cloth, and ices. All the streets of the main bazaar in Kabul are covered over with a crazy patchwork of gunny - bags as though fashioned by a futurist artists crazed with drinking too many bowls of bhang. As a result of these canopies the streets are like tunnels. They are dark, gloomy and reeking with the mingled aromas of all the choicest smells of Cairo, Constantinople, Damascus, Bagdad, Benares, and Bokhara. They are several miles in extent and usually packed with fierce looking wild tribesmen from every corner of Central Asia. Many of them regard the killing of an Unbeliever the surest way of going to Paradise. Often they go wild with religious fanaticism. When that happens to a man he is called a Ghazi, and he starts out with his dagger resolved to disembowel an Unbeliever. So it was a good thing that a part of the Amir's bodyguard always accompanied the party when they went to the Kabul bazaar

All the streets of the main bazaar in Kabul are covered over with a crazy patchwork of gunny - bags as though fashioned by a futurist artists crazed with drinking too many bowls of bhang. As a result of these canopies the streets are like tunnels. They are dark, gloomy and reeking with the mingled aromas of all the choicest smells of Cairo, Constantinople, Damascus, Bagdad, Benares, and Bokhara. They are several miles in extent and usually packed with fierce looking wild tribesmen from every corner of Central Asia. Many of them regard the killing of an Unbeliever the surest way of going to Paradise. Often they go wild with religious fanaticism. When that happens to a man he is called a Ghazi, and he starts out with his dagger resolved to disembowel an Unbeliever. So it was a good thing that a part of the Amir's bodyguard always accompanied the party when they went to the Kabul bazaar

Afghanistan - No. 39., Kabul extends for a mile and a half from east to west and a mile from north to south. It is hemmed in by barren mountains. Over the tops of these mountains runs a jagged, ruined ancient wall which looks like a miniature Great Wall of China. Sanitation in its modern sense is as unknown in Kabul as it was in Jerusalem before Allenby captured it. The present Amir is at work on a new capital in the fertile Chahardeh Valley midway between Kabul and his Summer palace in the Paghmam Hills twenty miles distant. This new city was planned by his grandfather, the great Amir Abdur Rahman

Afghanistan No. 49, The greatest ruler Afghanistan has had for many decades was Abdur Rahman. He conquered the country by winning the allegiance of the wild tribes. He built roads and opened up schools. But during the reign of the late Habib Ullah the schools were closed and the teachers put in prison. Some of the orthodox Mohammedan priests who had the ear of the Amir persuaded him that the schools were plotting against him. However, the new occupant of the throne has reopened them and established many more. Abdur Rahman did much to improve the country by introducing fine breeds of animals and agricultural products from other lands. Flocks form and main wealth of the nomad population. Among the products grown in some of the fertile valleys are wheat, barley, lentils, rice, millet, maize, turnips, potatoes, and other garden stuffs, tobacco, delicious melons and fruits of all kinds. The castor - oil plant grows everywhere and is widely used as a purgative by the Hakims or physicians who prescribe it for all ailments from sore eyes and liver complaints to rheumatism and baldness. There are barbers and others with complete lack of knowledge of anatomy who practice the art of surgery with much the same skill that one would expect a British bricklayer of blacksmith to exhibit

Afghanistan - No. 63., General Fakri Pasha, who represents the "Young Turks" at the Amir's Court, won considerable fame during the world war, first at the defense of the Dardanelles and then when transferred to the Arabian Desert to fight the forces of the King of the Hedjaz and Colonel Lawrence. He made his headquarters at Medina, the forbidden Moslem city where the Prophet's tomb is located. Although his hope was a forlorn one he managed to defend Medina right up to the end of the war, and when Turkey finally capitulated he hurled defiance at the Allies and declared that he and his followers at Medina would fight until the last man was dead. He persisted in this attitude until after the Turks signed the armistice. But some days later his colleagues convinced him that things were hopeless and he finally consented to surrender to the combined British and Arab forces. General Fakri is believed to weild [sic] a powerful influence at the Court of the Amir. He has the appearance of a straightforward blunt old solider, and is a charming man to meet

Afghan - No. 67; Dil Kusha Palace, the Amir's residence in Kabul, is a two story, semi - European structure. Around it is an inner and an outer fort, and between them a deep moat. Two regiments guard the palace day and night, one occupying the inner fort and the other the outer. The general effect when viewed from the balcony of the Foreign Office is a strange medley of orient and occident. Around the palace are beautiful gardens. The present Amir seems almost as fond of gardens as were his illustrious predecessors the Great Moghuls

Afghan - No. 69, Several miles east of Kabul is another palace on a rocky hill. Behind it loom jagged mountains. Beneath it lies the fertile valley of the Kabul River. In the distance is one of the Amir's rookeries shaped like a fort. The lamp posts on either side of the Buick are of foreign design, and look as though they might have supported too many courtiers who have dined well but not wisely. But Afghanistan is the strictest prohibition country on Earth. There is no "Three - Mile - Limit� law," yet it is bone - dry. Even if these lamp posts do not indicate it. Inside the palace are quaint European furnishings. It seems strange in a country where they make gorgeous oriental carpets that one should fine the most conventional of "Axminsters" in the royal palace. There also is a ping pong table. It's difficult to imagine Afghans playing ping pong

Afghanistan - 75 - , One of the most prominent objects in Kabul is a white Column - of - Victory in the boulevard leading to the Great Mosque. Despite the fact that the Afghans have been defeated in all three of their wars with British India, this column was erected to commemorate the "victory" of the Afghans over the British Empire in the last war. On either side of the monument is a statue of an ancient Afghan warrior in coat - of - mail. At night the monument is illuminated. The column is more particularly to commemorate the battle of that in 1919 where the British suffered a temporary reverse

WITH LAWRENCE IN ARABIA . In late 1917, Lowell Thomas, American war correspondent, went to the Middle East to cover the Arab Revolt against the Turks, led by a young Englishman, Col. T.E. Lawrence, the most romantic and most contradictory figure of his era. Now that Sam Spiegel and David Lean are bringing to the screen the story of "Lawrence of Arabia" , with Peter O'Toole in the title role, surrounded by an all-star cast, the pictures taken by Lowell Thomas and his photographer, Harry Chase, have special significance. Thomas's own captions are used here. LTh-17 Colonel Lawrence conferring with Commander D.G. Hogarth, one of his advisers at the Arab Bureau of Cairo

Jan 1, 1975; Dear Lowell: Our happiest wishes to you for 1975! It has to be a great year for us all, and especially you. Certainly it will be for Sonny and Tay and family. They'll have the ski place in Juneau this summer - so it's time for your return to the high camps of JIPP. Let's count on it - say in late July - Affectionately, Mel, Joan, Ross and Lance; View East across the Juneau ice field; M. M. Miller

Note: The enclosed two pictures were taken on the way to Atlin. This reflection is of a mountain on the shore of Taku Inlet one mile from Indian Point and about ten miles from Lake Atlin. Several people I have shown the reflection picture to have declared it a fake. They couldn't believe it possible to get such a perfect reflection, but they were wrong. I have another that is even more beautiful which I will send you as soon as I get a print of it. On this picture I have been unable to decide which part is the reflection and which isn't but I believe the lighter half is not the mirrored part because the detail of the trees seems a trifle plainer [photograph accompanied by a letter to Frances Ryan]

Leather trunk series - Fort Seward
Note: Letter describing pictures

The two enclosed pictures are of snapshots I took on my first visit to Haines and Fort Seward, June 26th [1916]. The one of the soldiers drilling was taken on the parade ground at the Fort with Portage Bay in the back ground. Two companies are stationed at this post with a total enrollment of about 200 men. The building to the right is the hospital, to the left the barracks of Company C. in between are some of the residences of married non-commissioned officers and extending out in the bay is the Fort dock with the "Peterson" tied along side [photograph accompanied by a letter to Frances Ryan]

This other snapshot is of an old prospector on his way back to the creeks after laying in a few week's supplies. Although a bachelor, who has lived for the past ten years out in the wilderness all alone, barely panning enough colors to pay for his grub, he seems to get a lot of joy out of life and rides along the mountain roads strumming on his guitar and singing as though he had the whole world by the horns [photograph accompanied by a letter to Frances Ryan]

The enclosed snapshot taken of four "Alaskan Mountaineers" ascending a snowbank on the way to the summit of the "A.B.," back of Skagway, is another in which the camera was tipped so that the perpendicularity of the grade was lost. It looks as though we were on an almost level stretch of snow but it really was so steep we had to sink our toes in several inches at each step to keep from taking a mile-a-minute ride to the bottom of the mountain [photograph accompanied by a letter to Frances Ryan] [descrption an except from letter]

Photograph from China Essay Contest Dinner with Note 5.11

Note: AWARD PRIZES AT CHINA ESSAY CONTEST DINNER Eighty distinguished guests, all of them especially interested in China and in Far Eastern affairs, gathered at the Ford Motor pavilion on September 18 for a formal dinner in honor of the Contest's judges, prizewinners, and the contest's financial sponsor, W.D. Pawley. Lowell Thomas presented his newscast as part of the banquet, over which he presided. Fred L. Black, director of the Ford pavilion, acted as host. Pherbia Thomas Thornburg, contest director, presented the first three prizes to Minerva S. Desing of Collingswood, N.J.; Richard E. Curl of Edison, O.; and Helen Averitt of Pasadena, Calif. The spacious Ford Executive Lounge was especially decorated with Chinese screens, tapestries, modern paintings and statuary. Table decorations were Chinese junks, night-blooming water lilies in natural wood bowls, and silk Chinese and American flags. Costumed Chinese girls gave corsages to women guests and boutonnieres to men. Guests entered through a Dragon Gate; as they sat at table they could see, through the great glass wall of the Lounge, the Ford pavilion terrace which for the occasion had been transformed into a Chinese garden at Autumn Festival time, with trees, a scenic backdrop, a compound wall, gay lanterns, and dainty costumed Chinese girls having tea. A Chinese orchestra played. Favors, supplied by the China Essay Contest, were handsome souvenir books especially published and bound in brocade treaty silk. In this photo (left to right) are: Lowell Thomas, Rear Admiral H. E. Yarnell and Pearl Buck

Lowell Thomas: Broadcasting [final broadcast]

NXP1868419-5/15/76-New York: Lowell Thomas signs off for the last time 5/15 as the longest running radio network program goes off the air after 46 years. The familiar "So long until tomorrow" became "So long for now" as Thomas completed his last five-minute news broadcast. The end of his broadcasting career does not mean retirement for Thomas, who is 84. He has written 54 books and has several more planned. UPI

Verso: Dear Lowell Thomas, This is a picture of our cabin in Cripple Creek. You once told me you were born there in 1893. This cabin is back of our theatre. I am on the extreme left of the picture. Each of the others were musicians and each had a job to do. They called me "Jimmy Gets" ( get-the- wood- and- water- boy ). Also actor - I hoped! Merry Christmas to you. [signed] Fred Stone

Note: Professor Taylor, Principal of the Victor High School, friend of my father, and a top flight educator. He's one of two of my teachers who actually gave me a licking. The other was a woman, an amazon who was my teacher in the 8th grade. She also was a great person and I'm sorry I've forgotten her name. I believe she later became a doctor in Fort Collins, Colorado. Professor Taylor was quite right in giving me that licking?

Note: July 25; Hi! Some pictures I thought you'd like to have (have sent copies to mother, too). Perhaps Sally would like to see them - many thanks for the new Bible-quite a change! Look forward to reading it. Life hectic, as usual. Am trying to get lots done around the house while Lowell is in California. We're all well-the children swimming like fish now-also enjoying the woods and stream-haven't worn my shoes for weeks! Lots of love, Tay

LOWELL THOMAS RETURNS FROM TIBET, Lowell Thomas, newscaster, waves a crutch as he leaves a Pan American World Airways plane at La Guardia Field, New York, Oct. 16, upon his return by air from a trip to Tibet. He was accompanied by his son, Lowell, Jr. (left). Thomas broke a thigh bone in a fall from a horse on a Tibetan mountain pass last summer. He said he believed Tibet, which has an army of 10,000 would accept outside help if attacked by Chinese Communists, 10/16/49

New York Bureau, THOMAS RETURNS FROM TIBET, NEW YORK: Lowell Thomas, explorer and radio commentator, is greeted by his father, Dr. Harry G. Thomas (right) as he and his son, Lowell Thomas, Jr., (left) arrive at La Guardia Field, Oct. 16. The Commentator was injured in a fall from his horse while riding in the Himalayas. He suffered a broken pelvis. From Karo Pass, 16, 700 feet above sea level, Thomas said he was carried on a litter to Gyantse, a six-day trip, and thence to the Indian border, a journey of some eight days. Thomas said the rulers of Tibet want to know if the U.S. will help them in the event of a Communist invasion. 10-16-49 (LG)

THOMAS LEAVES HOSPITAL, Lowell Thomas, noted CBS newscaster, today bade farewell to Assistant Director Phyllis M. Young (left) and supervisor Waveney Towey, as he left the Harkness Pavilion of the Columbia Presbyterian Medical Center, where he was operated on for a broken hip bone, suffered in a fall from a horse on his recent visit to the Dalai Lama in the Forbidden City of Lhasa, Tibet. He went from the hospital to his home in Pawling, N.Y., where he will complete his recovery, broadcasting from there daily on his CBS 6:45-7:00 PM, EST, news program

Note: from: Columbia Broadcasting System, INC. 485 Madison Avenue, New York 22, N.Y., Plaza I-2345; 1949: A Visit to Tibet A memorable moment in journalism took place in 1949 when CBS News Correspondent Lowell Thomas and his son penetrated the Himalayas and reached Lhasa, the forbidden city of Tibet, for an exclusive interview with the Dalai Lama. In this photo Mr. Thomas is seen with the family of the Dalai Lama with the Potala, the Dalai Lama's palace, rising in the background.

Note: PRESENTS TIBETAN SCROLL TO PRESIDENT: Lowell Thomas, Jr., son of the radio commentator, is shown in Washington, D.C., Nov. 9 [1949], with the Tibetan scroll he presented to President Truman. The scroll was brought from Tibet by the elder Thomas a few weeks ago. The scroll, bearing a message in Tibetan characters, handwritten with a piece of bamboo on a parchment from the bark of a tree, was presented to Thomas by two top officials of the Dalai Lama's government. Lowell Thomas, Sr., injured in a fall from a horse in Tibet, was brought home by a rescue team sent into Tibet by the Indian government.

This one, although large enough to carry twenty people or six horses, is so light that the boat-man can put it on his back and carry it upstream. And, that is only way of getting it up a river. Herd of Yak. This of course is the animal on which the Tibetan depends on so much. Without Yak it is doubtful there would be human life on the "roof of the world". Instead of saying "how do you do" or using some other greeting familiar to us, Tibetans exchange silk scarves. These they place over each others wrists. Tibetan artist. Art is an important part of Tibetan life. There are many artists. They were constantly at work decorating the innumerable monestaries or Lamaseries, also making pictures for homes and for public buildings. Monks recieving their noon-day allotment of barley flour. One out of every four males in Tibet becomes a Lama, a monk. So this could be considered one of the routine activities of Tibet. Tibetan monk blowing a trumpet on the roof of a monestery om tje capitol city of Lhasa. Some trumpets are made from human thigh bones. Others of great shells imported over the lofty mountains from China or India, and still longer trumpets -- some eight, ten, and twelve (-2-) feet long are made of brass. Trumpets and horns are beling blown from the roofs of the monasteries almost constantly.

Tibet: Trip to Dharamsala [Travis L. Fletcher and Katherine Cantwell]

The Director [Travis L. Fletcher] and his associate Mrs. Katherine Cantwell are greeted by the children at the Tibetan Nursery School in Dharamsala on the occasion of a recent visit. The usual salutation of the Bhudists [Buddhists] is in evidence. The sister [Tsering Dolma] of His Holiness stands to the right of Mr. Fletcher. She directs the work of this school which accommodates 600 children. AECTR [American Emergency Committee for Tibetan Refugees] has supported the nursery with medecines [sic], clothing, shoes and food, just one of four schools receiving similar help

Mrs. Katherine Cantwell, Assistant Field Director, AECTR [American Emergency Committee for Tibetan Refugees], with one of hundreds of Tibetan women who were recently evacuated from NEFA during the invasion of India by Communist China. Though depressed and disillusioned the Tibetans never complain, witness the happy expression on this woman's face. This photograph was taken in the Kulu valley in the far northern part of India where AECTR [American Emergency Committee for Tibetan Refugees] is furnishing medecines [sic] and other relief supplies

A small group out [of] approximately 5000 Tibetan refugees who were evacuated from NEFA during the recent invasion of India by Communist china. They managed to escape with only the clothes they wore and have since sought refuge in the interior of India, wandering aimlessly, bewildered, disillusioned and discouraged. Subject - Two scientists from the United Kingdom's Halley Bay Station on the Eastern coast of Antarctica explore the ice cliffs along the coast. Extreme winds, often reaching 100 MPH, and blowing snow carves natural sculptures into the thick ice mountains. Antarctica is the highest of thw World's seven continents with an average elevation of about 7,500 feet. It's also the coldest and windiest of the continents. The Soviet Union's Vostok Station recorded the world's coldest temperature of 126.9 degrees below zero Fahrenheit on August 24, 1960

22 November 1962, Congressman Poage of Texas, and Lowell Thomas, renown radio news commentator, partake of traditional Thanksgiving dinner at the enlisted men's chow hall at Advance Headquarters for Operations Deep Freeze at Harewood Christchurch, New Zealand. Note: Call PAN AMERICAN - Photographic Dept. Many years ago, in the thirties, Mr. Thomas helped you folks at Pan Am to launch the first passenger fligt around the world, from LaGuardia. NEW YORK BUREAU; PUTTING AN ODYSSEY ON FILM, CAIRO: - Globe-trotter Lowell Thomas, producing a film called "Seven Wonders of the World," stands before two ancient marvels in Egypt - the Great Pyramid of Cheops (background) and the Sphinx. The noted commentator and adventurer recently completed a globe-circling trip to 32 countries working on the film, the third "Cinerama" production. The modern odyssey covered 100,000 miles and the Cinerama crew worked with two airplanes and five directors; CREDTI (UNITED PRESS PHOTO) 11/18/55

Subject files: Cinerama (Seven Wonders of the World)

Lowell Thomas, producer of the third Cinerama adventure, "Seven Wonders of the World," examines a model of the Sphinx with pretty Eileen Salama. Miss Salama handled all the advance arrangements for the Cinerama expedition during its visit to one of the most remote corners of the world, Wadi Beihan in southern Arabia. There Cinerama camera men filmed a stampede of thousands of camels and were guests of honor at a banquet held by the fabulous Sherif Hussein

Fascinating Lake Baikal, in Central Siberia. It is the deepest in the world (almost a mile deep) and 353 miles long. 1800 species of plant and animal life have been identified; ¾ of them are found no place else on earth. It is a highlight of both the 8-day and 15-day Alaska Airlines tour. Intourist photograph

An alert photographer of the Winnipeg Free Press snapped this prize-winning photo which appeared on the front page of the Winnipeg Free Press, July 6th edition; This same stunt will be repeated at the State Fair of Oklahoma at Oklahoma City, September 24-29 when the Aut Swenson Thrillcade combined with star-studded hippodrome features will be presented before afternoon grandstand throngs

Sunset over "Spook Mountain" overlooking the mining camp at Slab Fork, W. Va.; Note: Two little colored boys talking one day at Slab Fork, W. Va. One pointed across the "holler." "See that there moun-tin" he asked his companion. "Dat's Spook Moun-tain" , "Why you call dat Spook Moun-tin?", "Cause'n I know a man went up thar one day, ad' he sayed, "Spook, cum git my wife." An when dat man went home his wide was jus' as daid as a dwag." After a moment's silence the little fellow continued, I bet iff'n you went over there an' say "Spook, cum git me," we never would see hide or hair of you again.......I bet there ain't a man in the whole Slab Fork 'ud dare go up that moun-tin and holler "Here Spook!"

FORD EXPOSITION BIDS GOODBYE TO ADMIRAL BYRD The Ford Exposition was host at New York's principal farewell banquet to Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd, about to leave on his third Antarctic Expedition, at the New York World's Fair. The banquet was organized by the Order of Adventures, and more than 200 national and international figures were guests. Left to right at the speakers' table are Phillips Carlin of the National Broadcasting Company; Captain Felix Riesenberg, retired naval officer, author and explorer; Senator Frederic C. Walcott of Connecticut; Frank E. Mason, vice president of the National Broadcasting Company; Mrs. Lenox Lohr; F.L. Black, in charge of the Ford Exposition; Mrs. Roy Chapman Andrews; Admiral Byrd; Lowell Thomas, famed radio commentator; Alice Roosevelt Longworth; Dr. Roy Chapman Andrews, director of the American Museum of Natural History; Mrs. Lowell Thomas; Major Lenox Lohr, president of the National Broadcasting Company; Mrs. Frank Mason; Col. Theodore Roosevelt; Leslie Bain, director of the Order of Adventures.

Subject files: The Explorers Club (Ford Exposition banquet for Vilhjalmur Stefansson)

Note: FORD HONORS STEFANSSON The Ford Motor Company gave a formal dinner in the Executive Suite of the Ford pavilion on August 23 in honor of the great Arctic explorer, scientist and author - Vilhjalmur Stefansson. Fred L. Black, Ford Exposition director, presided, and among the speakers were Sir Hubert Wilkins, Joseph Robinson and Reginald Orcutt. Scores of notables in the field of exploration and science attended. As guests entered the dining room Ford Information girls in fur parkas gave them flowers. Small polar bears were the table favors. In honor of Mr. Stefansson the Ford terrace, visible to the diners through the wall of clear glass, was decorated to represent an Arctic scene. A backdrop, illuminated by blue lights, showed an Eskimo family cooking dinner near an igloo, with open water, a floating iceberg and the aurora borealis in the distance. In the foreground was a set representing the interior of an igloo, containing a polar bear skin, a rifle and other trappings. Adjoining was a loaded dog sled, with a team of live huskies tethered nearby, squatting in artificial snow. In the foreground a man in parka and mukluks cooked his dinner on a primus stove. This photo shows Joseph Robinson, Vilhjalmur Stefansson, Sir Hubert Wilkins and Reginald Orcutt.

Note: FORD EXPOSITION HONORS SIR HUBERT WILKINS Fifty friends of Sir Hubert Wilkins, famous polar explorer, gathered in the Executive Suite of the Ford Exposition, New York World's Fair, on July 29. The occasion was a formal dinner given for Sir Hubert and Lady Wilkins by the Ford Motor Company. Sir Hubert had just returned from France (he was in Paris the day before it fell) and Britain. Fred L. Black, director of the Ford Exposition, welcomed the guests in behalf of the Ford Motor Company. Besides Sir Hubert speakers were Lowell Thomas and Joseph Robinson. Guests included distinguished members of the Explorers Club and others. In this photo: Sir Hubert Wilkins, Mr. Lowell Thomas

Subject files: First World Flight

Note: In 1924 eight U. S. Army airmen, years before there was a "U. S. Air Corps and then a U. S. Air Force" , in four bi-planes (Douglas World Cruisers), started out to circumnavigate the globe by air. It was the greatest international air race of all time. None of the planes from the six European countries that already had entered the race, succeeded in getting more than half-way around. One American plane, The Flagship, flown by Major Frederick Martin and Sgt. Al Harvey crashed in Alaska. ; These are the six flyers who made it all the way around, with L. T., historian of the flight, and Vi Moseley, for a time L. T.'s secretary. She had been secretary to Gen. Billy Mitchell, who had been rejected from the Army because his ideas were too far advanced. He knew air power would soon be predominant but his superiors, all Army Generals, were not sufficiently far-sighted enough to agree. This flight was one of the major mile-stones in the history of man, and actually launched the travel-by-air-era. World War II airmen with surplus World War II planes, launched the first aerial passenger service a year after the conclusion of this flight. America following their example in 1926. ; The names of the First World Flyers were: reading from left to right: - Lt. Leslie Arnold, who later helped Eddie Rickenbacker launch Eastern Airlines; Lt. John Harding; Lt. Erik Nelson, later a Vice President of Boeing and one of the men who launched SAS; Lt. Leigh Wade, who became a World War II Air Force General; Lt. Lowell Smith, who became the Second Commander of the First World Flight and several years later was killed in Arizona; and Lt. Henry H. Ogden, who became a civilian aviation expert [Lowell Thomas, second from right]
Verso: (for Pherbie) left to right

LIEUT. WADE'S DISABLED PLANE BROUGHT ALONGSIDE CRUISER RICHMOND IN NORTH ATLANTIC; This EXCLUSIVE PHOTO shows Lieutenant Leigh Wade's disabled plane, the "Boston" being brought alongside the cruiser Richmond after being towed by the larger ship by the destroyer Billingsley. Our photo shows one of the plane's crew on the pontoon prepared to keep the plane from smashing into the ship. Shortly after, the Richmond tried to lift the plane on board. It was then that the tackle broke, the Boston falling back into the water and being smashed so badly that it had to be destroyed. B 9-1-24

Subject files: Harrison Forman and Chairman Mao Tse-Tung [Zedong]

Harrison Forman with Chairman Mao Tse-Tung; Yenan, North China - 1944; Photo made during World War II when Harrison Forman was a War Correspondent based in Chungking, the wartime capital. Mr. Forman was the first American newsman invited to visit the regions controlled by the Chinese Communists in North China. His book, REPORT FROM RED CHINA, recounting his talks with the Red leaders, and travels with their troops in military actions against the Japanese, created a sensation when published in America. It was translated into fifteen foreign languages including Chinese

Verso: Harrison Forman with Chairman Mao Tse-Tung; Yenan, North China - 1944; Photo made during World War II when Harrison Forman was a War Correspondent based in Chungking, the wartime capital. Mr. Forman was the first American newsman invited to visit the regions controlled by the Chinese Communists in North China. His book, REPORT FROM RED CHINA, recounting his talks with the Red leaders, and travels with their troops in military actions against the Japanese, created a sensation when published in America. It was translated into fifteen foreign languages including Chinese

THEY PREPARE TO GET AHEAD: Stone Age savages of unexplored Sepik River area in New Guinea prepare for head-hunting battle against a rival tribe and make for a thrilling sequence in the first episode of the new television adventure series, "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas," which will be shown over the CBS television network on Tuesday, November 12, 8:00 to 9:00 P.M. EST. The series, which will consist of seven full-hour films in color of the adventures of Lowell Thomas and other explorers in such diverse places as New Guinea, the Arctic, Venezuela, the Australian Outback, and African desert and jungle, is being sponsored by the United Motors System and Delco-Remy divisions of General Motors. One film will be shown at specially-scheduled times once a month through May

EST. The savage tribesmen, who live exactly as they did 2,000 years ago and have no knowledge of common metals or other contrivances, depend on bow and arrow to kill rival neighbors for souvenir heads. ARCTIC PIONEERS REUNITE; New York, N. Y., August 31, 1957 - Four pioneers of Arctic exploration - Admiral Donald B. MacMillan, Sir Hubert Wilkins, Peter Freuchen and Col. Bernt Balchen - left Idlewild Airport with Lowell Thomas over the weekend on first step of a photography expedition to polar regions for new television adventure series, "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas," which will make bow over CBS-TV network early in November. This is first meeting of quartet who will retrace trails in icy northern wastes which they pioneered and study new techniques of living in Arctic, which is now important American line of defense. (Left to right are shown: Adm. Donald B. MacMillan, Sir Hubert Wilkins, Peter Freuchen, Lowell Thomas, Col. Bernt Balchen and Gilbert Ralston.)

TALL GIFT: Lowell Thomas accepts ceremonial gift from Rimshi Dote, one of the Tibetan district governors, who is almost seven feet tall, enroute to Lhasa, the forbidden capital of Tibet. Thomas and his son, Lowell Thomas, Jr., were the 7th and 8th Americans allowed to visit that strange country which forms the basis of Episode No. 4 in the CBS television series, "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas," (CBS-TV, Tuesday, February 25, 8:00-9:00 p.m., EST)

HORSES WIN OKAY: Lowell Thomas and party followed the ancient and treacherous caravan route from Sikkim over the high Himalayas to get to forbidden Tibet, which is the backdrop for the fourth installment of High Adventure with Lowell Thomas," which will be colorcast over the CBS television network Tuesday, February 25th, 8:00-9:00 p.m., EST. Thomas fondles his equine carrier which is most dependable form of transportation since Tibetans absolutely forbid travel by air, car, or even by carriage, or cart. As far as transportation is concerned, Tibet is a country without a wheel

OUTBACK BACKGROUND: A good idea of the roughness of the Australian Outback terrain which is featured in the fifth edition of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" (in color on CBS-TV, Monday, March 24th, 8:00-9:00 p.m., EST) can be obtained from this photo showing trucks of the Lowell Thomas expedition trying to find traveling space. Most sections of the vast desert, however, can be traversed only by camel. The Thomas troupe spent months in this forsaken land looking for the bones of the lost Australian-American explorer, Harold Bell Lasseter. The search was successful. The Lasseter story is the subject of the fifth "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" which is sponsored by the United Motors System and Delco-Remy division of General Motors

Subject files: High Adventure with Lowell Thomas (Tiger Hunt)

GOOD LISTENER----Lowell Thomas (right) takes some good advice from John Grisham [Jack Girsham?], who knows his way around the rugged country of northeast India, during filming in color of sixth edition of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" which will be televised on CBS network Saturday, April 19, from 9:00 to 10:00 p.m., EST. Grisham [Girsham?], carrying elephant rifle, was a most valued scout with the famous Merrill's Marauders during that unit's tussles with the Japanese in Burma in World War II. A hunt for wild elephants and man-eating tigers features this particular edition of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas," which is sponsored by the United Motors System and Delco-Remy Division of General Motors

BUILDING A BETTER TRAP----Natives in Assam Province of northeast India are in the process of constructing huge trap for man-eating tiger that has been attacking fellow villagers. Over 500 spearmen and "beaters" participated in the hunt for the striped beast which is featured in the next edition in color of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" (CBS-TV network, Saturday, April 19, 9:00 to 10:00 p.m., EST). Other stirring sequence in the hour-long show depicts capture and training of wild elephants. "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" is sponsored by the United Motors System and Delco-Remy Division of General Motors

POINTS THE WAY----Noted film director Willard Van Dyke points out next scene in action during filming of sixth episode (Tiger Hunt in India) of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" (in color over CBS-TV network, Saturday, April 19, 9:00 to 10:00 p.m., EST). Lowell Thomas and his production crew spent more than three months in the jungles of Assam Province in northeast India photographing live capture of a vicious man-eating tiger by 500 natives. Also to be seen in the film is round-up of wild elephants for conversion to domestic use. Mahouts on elephants in background actually "lasso" the wild pachyderms in same fashion as Western cowboys rope steers. Van Dyke won much acclaim for his production and direction of the documentary film, "The City"

PIQUED BY PEAK -- One of Alaska's imposing mountains is a background for Lowell Thomas as the intrepid explorer-author-producer gets ready to "shoot" scenes in full color for the initial installment of the new "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" TV series which will bow over the CBS television network on Wednesday, October 8th, from 8:00 to 9:00 p.m., Eastern Daylight Time. Entire show is devoted to the challenges and possibilities of America's newest state and last big frontier. "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" is presented by the united Motors System and Delco-Remy Division of General Motors

Flag is official emblem of the Explorers Club of New York. ICY INTRODUCTION - Lowell Thomas emerges from a crevasse in Alaska's immense glacial ice pack during "shooting" of first edition of the new series of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" color films set for showing over the CBS television network Wednesday, October 8th, 8:00 to 9:00 p.m., Eastern Daylight Time. Sun glasses, special skin ointment, etc. are necessary to protect the face and eyes from dangerous infra-red rays bouncing off the glaring snow. HIGH FLIERS - Daring every-day escapades of fearless Alaskan bush pilots are dramatically depicted in the first edition (Alaska-America's Last Frontier) of the new "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" video series in full color over the CBS television network Wednesday, October 8th from 8:00 to 9:00 p.m., Eastern Daylight Time. Here, Lowell Thomas disembarks on the tricky Alaska ice pack from a light plane piloted by Merrill Wien, one of the best-known of the Alaskan daredevils whose exploits will make armchair adventurers sit up and take notice. Because of the lack of railroads and highways, the plane is the most used transportation vehicle nowadays in the land of the midnight sun. "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" is sponsored by the United Motors System and Delco-Remy Division of General Motors

Subject files: High Adventure with Lowell Thomas (Danger Island)

DANGER FLIGHT - Lowell Thomas dons lifejacket before leaving by helicopter from the deck of the USS Point Defiance for first look at Danger Island (Puka Puka), tiny coral atoll in the South Pacific, which is the scene for the third edition of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" to be colorcast over the CBS television network, Monday, January 19th, from 10:00 to 11:00 p.m., EST. Later, Thomas landed on the island with 32 famous scientists to check reactions of the sun by outer space rockets during the solar eclipse of October 12th

Note: [press release] DANGER FLIGHT - Lowell Thomas dons lifejacket before leaving by helicopter from the deck of the USS Point Defiance for first look at Danger Island (Puka Puka), tiny coral atoll in the South Pacific, which is the scene for the third edition of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" to be colorcast over the CBS television network, Monday, January 19th, from 10:00 to 11:00 p.m., EST. Later, Thomas landed on the island with 32 famous scientists to check reactions of the sun by outer space rockets during the solar eclipse of October 12th

UNUSUAL ROLE - Lowell Thomas (back row, center) officiates as King Neptune during ceremonies initiating "pollywogs" (first-time crossers of the Equator) into "shellbacks" aboard USS Point Defiance, which carried him and 32 world-famed American scientists to remote Puka Puka, or Danger Island, in the South Seas for one of the most important projects of the International Geophysical Year. Colorful, exciting activities on the island are main feature of the third installment of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" coming to TV screens in full color over the CBS network Monday, January 19th, from 10:00 to 11:00 p.m., EST. "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" is sponsored by the United Motors System and Delco-Remy Division of General Motors

Colorful, exciting activities on the island are main feature of the third installment of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" coming to TV screens in full color over the CBS network Monday, January 19th, from 10:00 to 11:00 p.m., EST. "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" is sponsored by the United Motors System and Delco-Remy Division of General Motors

SHIP TO SHORE - On board USS Point Defiance in the South Seas, preparatory to debarking to the lonely isle of Puka Puka, or Danger Island, Lowell Thomas (r.) confers with Dr. Friedman, one of the leaders of the 32-man Naval Research Laboratory scientific expedition, which used the island as headquarters to study the sun during the October 12th solar eclipse. Activities of the scientists on this by-passed coral atoll inhabited by a few hundred Polynesians, who have had little or no previous contact with the outer world, make for dramatic contrast in the third edition in color of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas," which will be telecast over the CBS-TV network, Monday, January 19th, from 10:00-11:00 p.m., EST

Note: [press release] SHIP TO SHORE - On board USS Point Defiance in the South Seas, preparatory to debarking to the lonely isle of Puka Puka, or Danger Island, Lowell Thomas (r.) confers with Dr. Friedman, one of the leaders of the 32-man Naval Research Laboratory scientific expedition, which used the island as headquarters to study the sun during the October 12th solar eclipse. Activities of the scientists on this by-passed coral atoll inhabited by a few hundred Polynesians, who have had little or no previous contact with the outer world, make for dramatic contrast in the third edition in color of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas," which will be telecast over the CBS-TV network, Monday, January 19th, from 10:00-11:00 p.m., EST

HOWDY, FOLKS - Lowell Thomas waves "howdy" while standing beside a Nike-Asp rocket on board the USS Point Defiance which transported the explorer and 32 scientists to the lonely isle of Puka Puka, or Danger Island, in the South Seas, scene of the third edition of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" to be colorcast over the CBS-TV network Monday, January 19th, 10:00-11:00 p.m., EST under the auspices of the United Motors System and Delco-Remy Division of General Motors. Puka Puka, directly in the path of the October 12th solar eclipse, was used by the scientists as headquarters to study the sun under eclipse conditions as one of the most important projects of the International Geophysical Year. The "Sadie Thompson" rocket was one of the six fired 150 miles into outer space to observe the sun from that vantage point during the eclipse totality. Besides the activity on Danger Island, Samoa, Tahiti and other South Sea spots are featured in the forthcoming "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas"

The "Sadie Thompson" rocket was one of the six fired 150 miles into outer space to observe the sun from that vantage point during the eclipse totality. Besides the activity on Danger Island, Samoa, Tahiti and other South Sea spots are featured in the forthcoming "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas"

DANGER ISLAND HEADQUARTERS - This is the camp set up for 32 American scientists by the U. S. Navy on Puka Puka, or Danger Island, in the uncharted South Seas, scene of the third installment of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" (in color, CBS-TV, Monday, January 19th, 10:00-11:00 p.m., EST). One of the most important projects of the International Geophysical Year, scientists used jet-age instruments, including rockets launched 150 miles into outer space, to record activities of the sun during the October 12th eclipse. Navy frogmen were forced to blast a channel through dangerous reef to land supplies on the seldom-visited island. This and other dramatic incidents are featured in the "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" show, which is sponsored by the United Motors System and Delco-Remy Division of General Motors

EXOTIC BELLE - "Whiskey Johnnie" (that's her real name) Frisbie, half-native daughter of the legendary South Seas author, Rober Dean Frisbie, performs in an Hawaiian night club for opening scenes in the third episode of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" (in color, CBS-TV, Monday, January 19th, 10:00-11:00 p.m., EST). Thomas stopped off to interview "Whiskey Johnnie" about the little, unknown island of Puka Puka, or Danger Island, in the South Seas, where she was born and which is the backdrop for the next "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" show. The island, virtually cut off from civilization for centuries because its dangerous reef barred all vessels became the headquarters of a group of scientists from the U.S., transported there by the U. S. Navy to gather valuable knowledge about the sun during the October 12th eclipse. Six Nike-asp rockets launched 150 miles into space used in the observations. Titled "Danger Island," the Thomas one-hour film in color will highlight this and other dramatic events on the island during the IGY project. THEY GO TO HIS HEAD - Lowell Thomas, distinguished explorer and commentator whose next "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" TV show will be beamed over the CBS Television network on Friday, March 27th, 8:00-9:00 p.m., EST, is a hat collector. During his myriad wanderings around the world, Thomas has amassed an amazing collection of strange and exotic headgear which is stored in a special building on his estate near Pawling, N. Y. Thomas is shown here with a small part of his collection. Although he could get heady making a choice from the hundreds of hats he has on hand, Lowell, prefers the light gray Texas-type headpiece shown on the far right

ENDED RIGHT HERE - Back in the United States, Lowell Thomas points out the exotic island of Zanzibar, final port of call on a 3,500-mile ocean trip in an ancient Arabian dhow along the Arabian and East African coasts from Bahrein on the Persian Gulf. The exciting fourth installment of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" will be colorcast over the CBS television network Friday, March 27th, 8:00-9:00 p.m., EST, under the sponsorship of the United Motors System and Delco-Remy Division of General Motors. It took the sail-driven dhow a month to make the voyage. Besides life on the dhow, the next "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" also will display other thrill-packed sequences such as a falcon hunt in southern Arabia, a pearl diving expedition in the Persian Gulf, a turtle hunt along Africa's east coast and a novel bullfight in Zanzibar where the bull always wins!

A DAY WITH DAY - On a month-long, 3,500-mile trip by native dhow from the Persian Gulf to Zanzibar, theme of the fourth installment of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas" (in full color, CBS-TV network, Friday, March 27th, 8:00-9:00 p.m., EST), Thomas stops off at the forbidden port of Mukalla on the South Arabian coast to chat with Wendy Day, the daughter of famed Clarence ("Life with Father" ) Day, who is the only American woman of four white women in residence there. Miss Day, who is married to a British fisheries officer, will be seen in one of the sequences of the March 27th shows, which is sponsored by the United Motors System and Delco-Remy Division of General Motors

DHOW-AGER OF THE SEA - Ancient Arabian sailing vessel, or dhow, is tied up in the strange port of Mukalla in Southern Arabia while Lowell Thomas and his production crew photographed scenes for the fourth edition of "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas," which will be beamed over the CBS-TV network Friday, March 27, 8:00-9:00 p.m., EST. Following the northwest monsoon trade winds, the dhow, which is one of the silent stars of the March 27th show, made the 3,500-mile trip from Bahrein on the Persian Gulf to the spice island of Zanzibar off Africa's east coast in a month. Many strange ports of call visited by the dhow were covered by the Thomas cameramen and will be seen in the next "High Adventure with Lowell Thomas," which is sponsored by the United Motors System and Delco-Remy Division of General Motors

Dear Ed Heffron, Three of these pictures were taken on an expedition in Australia. The old boy with the white beard and the heavy eyebrows is an Australian Drover. He was a well known character in the Australian Outback. Which I had a copy of that one. I've forgotten what they call the little animals on my arm. They actually look like dragons, and evidently are rather rare. We encountered them deep in the interior of Australia when we were on an expedition. The man chatting with me in the picture where I'm sitting on the front of a Land Rover, is an Australian film producer named Lee Robinson who was directing the making of our film. Behind us is what the Australians consider one of the wonders of the world, Ayers Rock. They say it is the largest single rock in the world and is several miles in circumference. The one with the young lady was made in a palace in the Atlas Mountains, in Morocco. And the one where I'm sitting at a table with a mask beside me was made in what was known as the Belgian Congo on the shores of Lake Albert. Sincerely, Lowell Thomas; P.S. All the pictures were probably all taken in 1958

Manned Spacecraft Center, Houston, Texas Apollo 15 EVA photo-Astronaut David R. Scott, commander, standing on the slope of Hadley Delta, uses a 70 mm camera during Apollo 15 extravehicular activity (EVA) on the lunar surface. He is some 10.5 miles (or 17.5 kilometers) from the base of the Apennine Mountains seen in the background. Scott carries tongs in his left hand. The Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV) or Rover is in the background. This view is looking east

Manned Spacecraft Center, Houston, Texas Apollo 15 EVA photograph---Astronaut James B. Irwin, lunar module pilot, gives a military salute while standing beside the deployed U.S. flag during the Apollo 15 lunar surface extravehicular activity at eh Hadley-Apennine landing site. The flag was deployed toward the end of EVA-2. The Lunar Module "Falcon" is in the center. On the right is the Lunar Roving Vehicle. This view is looking almost due south. Hadley Delta in the background rises approximately 4,000 meters (about 13, 124 feet) above the plain. The base of the mountain is approximately 5 kilometers (about 3 statute miles) away. This photograph was taken by Astronaut David R. Scott, Apollo 15 commander

Hadley Delta in the background rises approximately 4,000 meters (about 13, 124 feet) above the plain. The base of the mountain is approximately 5 kilometers (about 3 statute miles) away. Manned Spacecraft Center, Houston, Texas Apollo 15 EVA photo----Astronaut James B. Irwin, lunar module pilot, walks away from the Lunar Roving Vehicle during the third Apollo 15 lunar surface extravehicular activity (EVA-3) at the Hadley-Apennine landing site. The Rover is parked a short distance from the rim of Hadley Rille. The far wall of the rille is in the distance at the extreme upper left. Irwin is holding the 500m Hasselblad camera in his left hand. This photograph was taken by Astronaut David R. Scott, commander

TAKES BIG TRIP TO SEE DODGERS; Having traveled nearly half way around the world to see his first professional baseball game and to study American sports, Abd Traboulsi, Director of Athletics at the American University of Beirut, Lebanon, was the guest of Branch Rickey June 20 when the Brooklyn Dodgers defeated the Pittsburgh Pirates. Other guests at the game were Commissioner "Happy" Chandler and Ford Frick, President of the National League. Mr. Traboulsi who hopes eventually to introduce American baseball to his native Lebanon, plans to spend the summer at Ann Arbor taking a course for physical directors at the University of Michigan. With the American University of Beirut for 20 years, Mr. Traboulsi has charge of the athletic program for 2500 students representing 40 nationalities comprising the largest American university overseas. The American University of Beirut is a member of the Near East College Association of which Lowell Thomas is National Chairman and Allen Dulles, President of the Board of Directors. Photo shows: (left to right: Red Barber, Mr. Traboulsi, Commissioner Chandler and Mr. Rickey

Announcement of gifts of $1,000,000 toward the three-year goal of $15,000,000 to rehabilitate and expand the eight members of the Near East College Association was made by Lowell Thomas, fund chairman, tonight at a dinner honoring Dr. Allen O. Whipple, eminent American Surgeon. Dr. Whipple leaves for Lebanon shortly as advisor to the new Dodge Medical Center of the American University of Beirut, one of the largest single objectives of the fund. Dr. Whipple, retiring this year from Columbia University and Presbyterian Hospital, received tributes for his career in medicine from many persons of prominence at the dinner attended by Hon. Joseph C. Grew, Former Undersecretary of State; Madame Bechara El-Khouri, wife of the President of Lebanon; Allen W. Dulles, President of the Near East College Association; George Wadsworth, U.S. Minister to Syria and Lebanon; Photo Gratis for immediate release courtesy fund for Near East College Assn. ; Photo shows: Left to right, Dr. Allen O. Whipple, Joseph C. Grew, Allen W. Dulles and Lowell Thomas.

SALUTE TO SARNOFF More than 1,000 leaders of science, industry, government and religion gathered in New York tonight (Sept. 30) for an unprecedented salute to Gen. David Sarnoff, father of American television and chairman of the Radio Corporation of America. Gen. Sarnoff, who started his communications career on Sept. 30, 1906 as an office boy for the Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company of America, was honored with a 60th anniversary dinner at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel. Three national organizations - Electronic Industries Association (EIA), the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), and the National Association of Broadcasters (NAB) - joined forces to co-sponsor the "Salute to David Sarnoff." Gen. Sarnoff receives a gold medallion from toastmaster Lowell Thomas, while Vincent Wasilewski, president of NAB, holds a scroll citing Sarnoff accomplishments. At right is Frederick R. Kappel, chairman, American Telephone and Telegraph Company. At rear, from left, are Dr. Jerome Wiesner, provost and dean of Massachusetts Institute of Technology, representing IEEE; William S. Paley, chairman, Columbia Broadcasting System, representing NAB; and Walter K. MacAdam, vice president of IEEE. Altho' LT had left N.B.C. and gone over to CBS 20 years before this event Gen. Sarnoff asked him to be the toastmaster.

LOWELL THOMAS RECEIVES AMERICAN LEGION PUBLIC RELATIONS AWARD - Veteran reporter and commentator Lowell Thomas is presented the 1972 American Legion National Commander's Public Relations Award by National Commander John H. Geiger, of Des Plaines, Ill., at the Legion's annual Public Relations Luncheon held March 1, 1972. Newsman Thomas was cited for "his pioneering efforts in the audio visual field as a commentator and lecturer on our world" and for bringing to the people of the world "a greater understanding of diverse lands and cultures." The Legion's Public Relations Luncheon was held in conjunction with the organization's 12th annual Washington Conference, February 27 - March 3. Shown Left to Right are: National Commander John H. Geiger; Auxiliary National President Bertha Parker; Lowell Thomas; U.S. Secret Service Director, James J. Rowley; Legion National Adjutant, William F. Hauck

Lowell Thomas Honored by his college fraternity Lowell Thomas, famous author, news commentator and world traveler, smiles happily after receiving the 1938 Man of the Year Award from his college fraternity, Kappa Sigma. The presentation was made Friday evening, December 9, before 300 members of the fraternity at the Merchants and Manufacturers Club in Chicago. Hill Blackett, Chicago and New York advertising agency president, made the presentation, and Wesley W. Kergan, San Francisco attorney and Worthy Grand Scribe of Kappa Sigma, registers an expression of satisfaction as the fraternity has singled out another of its members for honor. Thomas was given this award after nation-wide balloting for his iron man feats as an author, adventurer and consistent accuracy in news commentating for over eight years on radio and screen.

World Adventure Series, Detroit, George F. Pierrot Lowell Thomas, principal speaker at a 1973 Detroit Press Club dinner commemorating the 40th birthday of the World Adventure Series, greets his friend George Pierrot, who founded the Series at Detroit's civic art museum in 1933. Thomas has been a member of the Series Board of Directors since its founding. Thomas, in behalf of friends and associates, presented Pierrot the portrait shown in the background, painted by the noted artist John Coppin. The World Adventure Series pioneered travel-adventure color movies in auditoriums and on television and has won many world-wide awards. The Detroit Press Club dinner was arranged by Leonard R. Barnes, author, world traveler and editor of Michigan AAA's monthly travel magazine, MICHIGAN LIVING

Verso: World Adventure Series, Detroit, George F. Pierrot Lowell Thomas, principal speaker at a 1973 Detroit Press Club dinner commemorating the 40th birthday of the World Adventure Series, greets his friend George Pierrot, who founded the Series at Detroit's civic art museum in 1933. Thomas has been a member of the Series Board of Directors since its founding. Thomas, in behalf of friends and associates, presented Pierrot the portrait shown in the background, painted by the noted artist John Coppin. The World Adventure Series pioneered travel-adventure color movies in auditoriums and on television and has won many world-wide awards. The Detroit Press Club dinner was arranged by Leonard R. Barnes, author, world traveler and editor of Michigan AAA's monthly travel magazine, MICHIGAN LIVING

Pierrot, the Series' founder. Lowell Thomas and George Pierrot are shown at the speakers' table. LOWELL THOMAS RECEIVES AMERICAN LEGION PUBLIC RELATIONS AWARD - Veteran reporter and commentator Lowell Thomas is presented the 1972 American Legion National Commander's Public Relations Award by National Commander John H. Geiger, of Des Plaines, Ill., at the Legion's annual Public Relations Luncheon held March 1, 1972. Newsman Thomas was cited for "his pioneering efforts in the audio visual field as a commentator and lecturer on our world" and for bringing to the people of the world "a greater understanding of diverse lands and cultures." The Legion's Public Relations Luncheon was held in conjunction with the organization's 12th annual Washington Conference, February 27 - March 3. L to R: Ralph Bates, Aide to the National Commander; James C. Watkins, Legion Director of Public Relations; The Rev. Edward L. R. Elson, Chaplain of the Senate, Lowell Thomas.

Caption: August 21, 1938. SENATOR POPE GUEST AT SUMMER WHITE HOUSE. Pawling, N.Y. - President Roosevelt with Sen. James P. Pope (left), administration supporter recently defeated in the Idaho primaries for re-nomination, as they watched a game between Lowell Thomas's "Nine Old Men" and the "White House Purgers" here, August 21. Senator Pope may run as an independent. He told newsmen he and the President touched briefly on the possibility of his re-entering the field

Note: DEFEATED IDAHO SENATOR DISCUSSES FUTURE PLANS WITH THE PRESIDENT, HYDE PARK, N.Y. - Lowell Thomas, author and radio commentator; Senator James J. Pope of Idaho, and President Roosevelt, photographed (left to right) after attending a baseball game between Mr. Thomas's "Nine Old Men," and the "New Deal Purgers," composed of White House correspondents, photographers and Secret Service Agents, near here on August 21. Both before and after the game, the Chief Executive and the Senator conferred on the advisability of the latter running independently against Representative D. Worth Clark, the choice of the Democratic Party for Senate

Subject files: Skiing (ski trophy in honor of Vic Constant)

[PDF] Note: I've been going through some thousands of pictures, selecting illustrations for the second volume of my autobiography. I gave this trophy in honor of Captain Vic Constant, coach of the West Point ski team back in the late thirties or early forties. Vic was killed when he was making a preliminary run down the Taft Trail in New Hampshire. It was the day before he was to have raced in the Nationals. He was a friend of mine, and much admired by all of us who were active in skiing at the time; Sincerely, Lowell Thomas; To Athletic Director of West Point, West Point, Madeline Salvani c.o Athletic Director U.S. Military Academy West Point, New York; 914-938-3303 (Lt. Gen. Sidney Berry) Captain McPhail - 938-4011, Maj. Campbell, Captain Hansen

Mead of New York is pictured fanning Vice-President Wallace after the V-P crossed the plate with a run in the second inning of their annual game here in Washington. Lowell Thomas captained the "Nine Old Men" team, while Rep. Ham Fish of New York, led the "Statesman" team. The game played for charity, lasted eight innings and was won by the "Statesmen" by a score of 15-14; M-6-3-41..1240PM

(Tunney Batting); Boxer Tunney a Slugger? New Canaan, Conn.Though his form can be described by a word that begins with an "L" and ends with a "Y" (not lovely), retired heavyweight king -- now columnist, Gene Tunney, is shown belting out a clean hit as his Fourth Estate "Connecticut Nutmegs" met commentator Lowell Thomas's "Nine Old Men" in a charity soft ball game yesterday. That's Thomas behind the bat. Note Gene's left foot "in the bucket." It would bring a nervous breakdown for any baseball manager. The Tunney bunch won 10-9

INSTRUCTIONS TO THE UMPIRE; Poundridge, N.Y. --- Not in the least disturbed by the declaration of umpire Anna May Wong that she "knew less than nothing" about baseball, Lowell, Thomas undertakes to explain the difference between a strike and a ball to the actress before the start of the game between his "Nine Old Men" and George T. Bye's "Prehistoric Sluggers" in Flaucher's Meadows August 15 for the benefit of the local volunteer fire department. Apparently he did a good job, for the "Nine Old Men" won by a score of 15 to 12. Members of both teams were well-known persons from literary and entertainment circles. 0-8/16/37 8

1. Sigiriya Rock The photograph show the famous Sigiriya Rock in Ceylon. The massive granite rock, which rises to a height of 600 ft., was converted into a fortress by a King named Kasyapa in the 5th century A.D. The King built a palace, baths, pavilions and a storage tank on the for acres of ground at the summit of the rock. A feature of the Sigiriya Rock is its frescoes which are considered masterpieces of art. The frescoes portray beautiful damsels presumably from King Kasyapa's Court.

The two Chinese airmen are attached to the Ninth Air Force as observers for the Chinese Air Force

The two Chinese airmen are attached to the Ninth Air Force as observers for the Chinese Air Force

Flying Officer Robert Joseph Campbell, D.F.C., of Pawling, N.Y., who was recently awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross while serving with the Royal Canadian Air Force in Britain as an air gunner. TOP-FLIGHT TRIO -Ranking members of the Fighting Corsairs Marine squadron, who between them have accounted for 60 Japanese planes, are shown here. At the left is First Lieutenant Robert M. Hanson of Newtonville, Mass., who was declared missing in action after downing his 25th enemy plane, one short of the American record. In the center is Captain Harold L. Spears of Ironton, O. [Ohio], who has downed 15 planes. At the right is Captain Donald N. Aldrich of Chicago, with 20 planes to his credit. The party was held in an Arab's barn which had been turned into an Officer's Club. Slides found with photographic prints: Lowell Thomas (Antarctica - from Cape Town to McMurdo Station, 1963): slide 1: Rear Admiral James R. Reedy and Lowell Thomas prepare to board one of the LC-130s of VX-6, Air Development Squadron, for the non-stop flight from Cape Town, South Africa to McMurdo Station, Antarctica; slide 2: Crews of both LC-130s shortly before departure on historic flight (non-stop) from Cape Town, South Africa to McMurdo Station, Antarctica. Left to right: front row - Lieutenant Commander Richard G. Dickerson, plane commander of lead plane, Rear Admiral James R. Reedy, Commander Task Force Forty Three, Commander George R. Kelly, Commanding Officer Air Development Squadron (VX-6), and Lieutenant Commander William B. Kurlak, plane commander of second plane; slide 3: Rear Admiral James R. Reedy, Lowell Thomas and pilots of VX-6 discuss plans for the non-stop flight by two LC-130s from Cape Town to McMurdo Station, Antarctica. Left to right: Lieutenant Commander Richard G. Dickerson, Lowell Thomas, Rear Admiral James R. Reedy, Commander Task Force 43, Lieutenant Commander Donald E. Miller and Commander George R. Kelly, Commanding Officer of Air Development VX-6; slide 4: The two LC-130s of VX-6, Air Development Squadron, ready to taxi out for take-off for the non-stop flight from Cape Town to McMurdo Station, Antarctica; slide 5: LC-130 aircraft #148320 of Air Development Squadron VX-6 at Naval Air Station, Rota, Spain where two of the squadron planes stopped for a crew rest during the flight to McMurdo Station; slide 6: LC-130 #148318 sits at the end of the running in preparation for take-off on the non-stop flight from Cape Town to McMurdo Station, Antarctica; slide 7: Rear Admiral James R. Reedy and Lowell Thomas
